commands.summary: Check this agent's messages
commands.usage:
orca orchestration check [--terminal <handle>] [--run <run_id>] [--ack <delivery_id>] [--unread | --peek | --all] [--types <type,...>] [--format] [--wait] [--timeout-ms <n>] [--retry-request <id>] [--json]
  default: return the bound Run's oldest unread FIFO batch and mark it handled.
  --ack: optional; acknowledges a batch from an older Orca that does not mark it.
  --peek: return only unread messages without marking them read.
  --all: return recent messages for the handle; does not mark read.
  --wait: block until a matching message arrives or --timeout-ms expires.
          Emits JSON keepalive lines to stderr every 15s so the caller can
          tell the process is alive. `_keepalive` is unrelated to heartbeat
          messages; `_heartbeat` remains as a deprecated compatibility alias.
          Filter with `jq "select(._keepalive|not)"` when merging streams.
notes: On Windows PowerShell, quote comma-separated type filters, e.g. --types "worker_done,escalation".

--types is the wake condition for --wait; a returned Delivery is always the whole FIFO batch, so it is never filtered by type. Without --wait it has no effect on consuming checks. Only --peek and --all filter their rows.
--format renders the returned rows as local text only; it never writes to another terminal.

A consuming check marks the batch it returns as handled, so the next check returns newer mail; no --ack is needed. Several --wait calls may wait on one inbox; waiting reserves nothing, listeners woken by the same arrival get the same Delivery, and --ack of a handled Delivery is a no-op. Consuming checks belong to the agent itself. A script that only watches the inbox must use --peek (including --peek --wait) and must never --ack, or it takes mail the agent never sees. If a check response was lost, rerun it with the --retry-request it printed to get the same batch. To find mail after losing context, run orca orchestration inbox --terminal <mailbox> --limit <n> --full and name the mailbox: run:<run_id> for a coordinator's bound Run, or dispatch:<dispatch_id> for a worker, including mail it read before it bound a helper Run.

A Dispatch created by orchestration dispatch reads from its adopted terminal with worker status unsupervised.
Output stays readable after the terminal is released, including an automatic release after worker_done.
A returned cursor is pinned to the exact source; start a fresh read if Orca reports source_changed.

commands.summary: Release the terminal of one settled supervised worker
notes: Post-completion cleanup for a settled (succeeded or failed) worker; closes only the exact coordinator-owned agent terminal of that worker.
A settled Dispatch created by orchestration dispatch has no owned terminal resource and is reported retained without process action.
An inspectable output archive is preserved before the terminal closes, so worker-read still returns output afterwards.
Never closes setup terminals, configured tabs, reused or pre-existing terminals, terminals the user kept open, or unproven identities.
Idempotent: repeating the call reports already_released. Only release_unknown exits 1; retained, release_pending, and already_released exit 0.

On a runtime that advertises orchestration.worker-auto-release.v1, an accepted worker_done already schedules this release about 2 minutes later (autoReleaseAt in worker-show and worker-list); call it only to release sooner or to clear a worker-keep-open. Chat workers follow autoReleaseAt too. autoReleaseAt is absent while its agent works again, and set afresh when it next goes idle.

commands.summary: Inspect one supervised worker Dispatch
notes: A Dispatch created by orchestration dispatch is shown as unsupervised and reports the exact adopted terminal when its identity is still provable.

observation.agentWait names a worker parked on a prompt only a human can answer, with the evidence that proved it (hook, prompt-text, or title). Null means Orca looked and found no wait. An absent field means it never looked — an older host, an unverifiable worker identity, an unreadable pane, or an agent probe that did not answer in time — and never means the worker is not waiting. A waiting worker is healthy, not failed.

commands.summary: Start one supervised worker on the Run home or a connected Orca server
notes: With --spec and no bound Run, a coordinator gets a new Run bound to it, named after the Task title; the receipt names the Run it created or joined.
Current and existing worktrees never rerun setup; a fresh agent terminal is created unless --terminal is explicit.
When reusing --terminal, pass --worktree for that terminal; current means the coordinator worktree.
Reusing a settled worker's terminal with --terminal before its autoReleaseAt cancels that automatic release; after it, the start is refused while the release runs.
A terminal the user kept open takes --terminal work and stays kept open.
--agent takes an Orca agent id enabled on the worker server, such as claude, codex, cursor, antigravity, muse, zcode, opencode, or opencode2.

--model supports Claude, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity, Grok, and Muse opaque provider model ids; --effort requires --model. OMP accepts --model only; --effort is unsupported. Neither can combine with --terminal. OpenCode model selection requires an existing worktree, a verified execution-host CLI, and an available model; effort is unsupported. Other agents, including zcode, launch with the model from their own config.
Finished workers close on their own unless started with --keep-open; a worker started in a new worktree (new-child or new-top-level) is kept open, so release it when no one will use its chat.
New worktrees use agent-first creation and default --setup to run. Repository start-immediately runs setup beside the agent; wait-for-setup gates agent readiness and task input.
New worktrees without --name get the name Orca gives an unnamed workspace; the receipt names it. Servers older than this change still require --name.

Creation flags (--name, --repo, --base-branch, --display-name, --comment, --setup) are rejected for current/existing worktrees. Use exact --repo on the selected server; project/host convenience routing remains on worktree create.

How the worker runs follows the user's own setting for new agent tabs; there is no flag for it and no caller needs to ask. A dispatch the setting cannot apply to still starts, so the placement, agent, and launch options passed here are always the ones honoured.

Drive every worker the same way whichever way it was started: the same orchestration verbs, the same handle. Mail, dispatch, worker-show, worker-read and the whole lifecycle behave identically. The start receipt records which one ran, for operators and telemetry.

Not every worker has a terminal. Read output with worker-read --source auto or --source transcript, which always work; --source terminal is refused when there is none, and orca terminal verbs do not accept every worker handle. Nothing above needs you to know which kind you have — the orchestration verbs cover all of them.
--on selects only the worker server; the Run and this command remain on the current Orca server.
Remote current and new-child are invalid; discover an exact remote selector or use new-top-level.
--retry-of needs --task naming the failed Task (--spec creates a new one) and does not inherit placement; repeat the intended --on/worktree and --agent/terminal choices.
--spec-file reads the spec from a file (relative to the current directory) or stdin (-) on this machine, so quotes and backticks need no shell escaping.
--keep-open keeps the worker open after it finishes, as worker-keep-open does right after start.

The call exits 0 for ready, and in the concise view for a start whose turn was not yet observed (--full exits 1 for anything but ready). Failed or outcome_unknown exits 1 and JSON includes stage/failedStage, setup, effects, residualResources, and recovery commands when needed.

commands.summary: Fence one Dispatch and stop its supervised agent terminal and its helpers
notes: A Dispatch created by orchestration dispatch is fenced without closing its unsupervised terminal process.
processAction closed_agent_terminal means Orca issued the close (do not also run terminal close); stop_unknown exits 1 and may still report it when the agent exit was not proven.
Also stops every helper it started and theirs, listed in helpers; a helper the user kept open is listed and keeps running.
Never deletes the worktree, setup terminal, configured tabs, or unrelated processes.

commands.summary: Export the active browser tab as PDF
Validate a plugin, render each components panel once on this machine (unsandboxed: only for code you trust), and statically check each custom editor
notes: Not sandboxed: this runs the plugin's code on this machine with your user's full access, outside Orca's plugin sandbox. Check only code you trust.

Validates like `orca plugin validate`, then mounts each `ui: "components"` panel in Node against a stand-in host with the capabilities the manifest declares, and reports runtime errors (with file:line), layouts Orca would refuse, and props it would drop.
Runs on the `node` on PATH when it is 20.6 or newer, else on the Node built into Orca. It does not reach the Orca app.
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 a panel failed to render or an editor failed its static check (plugin_check_failed), 2 the plugin is invalid (plugin_invalid).

commands.summary: Scaffold a new Orca plugin from a template
notes: Writes into a new or empty folder (a .git folder is allowed) and never overwrites; it runs no Git, package install or plugin code.
theme, terminal-theme, icon-theme, syntax and language-pack are content only: loading them never needs approval.
editor and panel run code in a sandboxed frame: loading them prints the access they ask for and needs --approve.
components is a panel written in TSX with Orca components and no build step; it also writes the editor typings to .orca/types (see `orca plugin types`).

worker-panel is a components panel plus its own TypeScript worker (`main`): requests, posts and storage typed by one src/protocol.ts, with panel and worker tests for `orca plugin test`. It needs --approve to load.
hook is a worker-only guard on `terminal.send` that refuses dangerous commands and fails closed (`onError: "deny"`), with a test for `orca plugin test`. It needs --approve to load.

The id defaults to the folder name. Leave out --publisher: Orca names the publisher after the repository owner (or `local` for a folder). Pass it only to support Orca older than 1.4.246, and then it must be that owner.
Runs on the machine that runs this command; it does not reach the Orca app.
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 error, 2 the plugin is invalid (plugin_invalid), 3 approval is needed (approval_required or approval_stale).

commands.summary: Fire a test event at a development plugin's worker and open panels
examples: orca plugin dev emit acme.notes agent.status.changed --data '{"workspaceId":null,"paneKey":"p1","state":"done","receivedAt":1}' --json
notes: Runs the worker's `orca.events.on` handlers and the plugin's open panels' `orca.on` handlers without the real trigger, under the normal rules: the plugin must be an approved development plugin granted the event's capability. The worker hears it when it lists the event in contributes.events (it starts if it is not running); an open panel hears it once it has subscribed. It is refused when nothing listens.
--data is the payload as JSON, checked against the event's schema (the host API reference lists them). An unknown event is refused with the list of events.
Prints `{ pluginKey, event, delivered: { worker, panels } }`: whether the worker got it and how many open panels did. Handler errors go to `orca plugin logs` and `orca plugin dev watch`.
Installed plugins are refused; load the folder with `orca plugin dev load` first.

commands.summary: Run a hook through a development plugin's worker and print what the chain decided
notes: Runs the worker's `orca.hooks.on` handlers with that plugin as the only one in the chain, under the same deadline and checks as a real hook; nothing in Orca acts on the result. The plugin must be an approved development plugin listing the hook in contributes.hooks.

--data is the hook's event as JSON (the host API reference lists them). Prints `{ pluginKey, event, decision }`, where decision is `{ kind: 'continue', event }` or `{ kind: 'deny', reason }`. A timeout or throw counts as passing and shows in `orca plugin logs`.

commands.summary: Open DevTools for a plugin's open panels and editors
notes: Desktop app only: opens one detached DevTools window per open frame. Console errors and uncaught exceptions also reach `orca plugin logs` without it.
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 error, 2 the plugin is invalid (plugin_invalid), 3 approval is needed (approval_required or approval_stale).

commands.summary: Load a plugin folder into Orca as a development plugin
notes: Adds the folder to Settings → Plugins → Development folders on the Orca host; it overrides an installed plugin with the same key.
Orca reloads the plugin when its files change. For an approved panel, editor or worker, later code edits run without asking again; new access does not.

.ts, .tsx, .mts and .jsx files load without a build step. When the folder uses them (or components panels) and is on this machine, this also refreshes its .orca/types typings, like `orca plugin types`.

Content-only plugins (themes, icons, syntaxes, translations) need no approval. Anything that runs code or acts in Orca fails with approval_required, which lists exactly what it would be granted, why, and the command to re-run with --approve <fingerprint>. The fingerprint is bound to that plugin, version, files and access; anything different needs a new one.
Without approval the folder stays loaded but nothing in it runs.
With --environment the folder is a path on that Orca server; pass it absolute.
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 error, 2 the plugin is invalid (plugin_invalid), 3 approval is needed (approval_required or approval_stale).

commands.summary: Reload development plugins now, or one folder and re-check its approval
notes: Orca already reloads on file changes; use this when a change was missed (network or WSL folders) or after changing commands or shortcuts, which need a new approval.
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 error, 2 the plugin is invalid (plugin_invalid), 3 approval is needed (approval_required or approval_stale).

commands.summary: Call a development plugin's worker handler the way a panel's plugin.request does
examples: orca plugin dev request acme.notes notes.list --json
notes: Runs the handler the worker registered with `orca.panels.handle(name, …)` through the same bridge an open panel's `plugin.request` uses: the plugin must be an approved development plugin with `main`, and its worker starts if it is not running.

--data is the input as JSON; without it the handler gets null, as `plugin.request(name)` sends. --panel sets the caller panel id the handler sees (default `orca-cli`); --timeout-ms is how long the handler may take (default 30000, at most 120000).

Prints `{ pluginKey, name, result }`. A handler error fails with `plugin_request_failed` and the worker's code in `requestCode` (`unknown_method` when nothing handles the name, `timeout`, `unavailable`, or the code the handler threw).
Installed plugins are refused; load the folder with `orca plugin dev load` first.

commands.summary: Remove a development folder from Orca
notes: Never needs approval. An installed plugin with the same key comes back, needing its own approval if access differs.

commands.summary: Load a plugin folder, then stream its logs and reloads until Ctrl-C
notes: The inner loop: loads the folder like `orca plugin dev load` (refreshing its .orca/types), then prints each log line its panels, editors and worker write, every reload a save causes, and status changes such as errored or invalid with the error.

A first load that needs approval, run in a terminal without --json, shows the grants and asks `Approve and load? [y/N]`; yes loads it with that fingerprint and keeps watching. Anything else, --json or no terminal (agents, pipes) fails like `orca plugin dev load` (exit 3, with the re-run command).
When an edit asks for new access it prints the `orca plugin dev reload <dir> --approve <fingerprint>` command to run from another shell; this one keeps watching.
Ctrl-C unloads the folder (unless it was loaded before this command) and exits 0; a second Ctrl-C exits at once. If the connection to Orca drops it says so and exits 1.

--check runs `orca plugin check` after the load and after each reload and prints the result inline (one `check` event with --json; it fails while Orca does not run the plugin, such as pending approval, even if the panels render). Like `orca plugin check` it runs the plugin's code on this machine, unsandboxed, so use it on code you trust; it needs a local folder.

--shot <out-dir> opens one panel in the right sidebar once (the first, or --shot-panel <id>; an unknown id fails at start), then after the load and each reload that leaves the plugin running saves a PNG of it, like `orca plugin shot`, to <out-dir>/<plugin-key>-<panel>.png (overwritten; a `shot` event). It never switches the sidebar again: while you show another tab or close the sidebar it skips, with one `shot_skipped` event per time away, and resumes when the panel is back. With --check, the check runs first. Needs the Orca desktop app.

--json prints one JSON object per line: `loaded`, `log`, `reloaded`, `status`, `approval`, `check`, `shot`, `shot_skipped`, `warning`, `disconnected`, `unloaded` (field `type`). A failed first load prints the usual error envelope instead, on one line.

Content-only plugins (themes, icons, syntaxes, translations) need no approval. Anything that runs code or acts in Orca fails with approval_required, which lists exactly what it would be granted, why, and the command to re-run with --approve <fingerprint>. The fingerprint is bound to that plugin, version, files and access; anything different needs a new one.
With --environment the folder is a path on that Orca server; pass it absolute.
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 error, 2 the plugin is invalid (plugin_invalid), 3 approval is needed (approval_required or approval_stale).

commands.summary: Disable a plugin
notes: Never needs approval.

commands.summary: Enable a plugin; code and capabilities need --approve
notes: Content-only plugins (themes, icons, syntaxes, translations) need no approval. Anything that runs code or acts in Orca fails with approval_required, which lists exactly what it would be granted, why, and the command to re-run with --approve <fingerprint>. The fingerprint is bound to that plugin, version, files and access; anything different needs a new one.
Enabling a plugin that is already approved and running needs nothing; re-enabling a disabled plugin that runs code needs --approve again.
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 error, 2 the plugin is invalid (plugin_invalid), 3 approval is needed (approval_required or approval_stale).

commands.summary: Show what a plugin folder contributes, the access it asks for, and its content hash
notes: Validates like `orca plugin validate`, then hashes the files the way install does.
Use it to show your user exactly what a plugin would be allowed to do before loading it.
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 error, 2 the plugin is invalid (plugin_invalid), 3 approval is needed (approval_required or approval_stale).

commands.summary: List plugins on the Orca host with their status and access level
notes: Status is running, idle, pending (waiting for approval), disabled, errored or invalid; dev marks development folders.

commands.summary: Print the recent log lines of a plugin
notes: Shows the last lines a plugin worker printed and its activation errors.

commands.summary: Show a plugin's panel in Orca's right sidebar, or open a file in its editor
notes: Without --panel it shows the plugin's first panel, opening the right sidebar if it is closed. --editor opens the file in the plugin's first custom editor that takes it, in the workspace that holds the file (its real path counts, so /tmp and /private/tmp match); when none does, Orca opens the file's folder as a folder workspace and opens it there.

Changes only what Orca shows: it never brings the window forward or takes focus. It leaves Settings for the workspace behind it; for a panel, other full-page views and a window with no workspace fail with no_workspace.
The plugin must be running or idle (approved and enabled); a pending plugin fails and says how to approve it.
Desktop app only: a server with no window (`orca serve`) refuses it. With --environment, --editor takes an absolute path on that host.
Use it to show your user the panel you just built; `orca plugin shot` captures it for you.

commands.summary: Print the catalog release entry for a plugin folder's committed HEAD
notes: Validates like `orca plugin validate`, then hashes the files of HEAD (not the working tree) the way install does, and prints the `releases` entry to paste into orca-catalog.json, plus the `source.path` when the plugin is a subdirectory of its repository.
Offline; runs only local read-only Git and never runs plugin code. Uncommitted changes are left out, with a note.
Fails with plugin_invalid when the folder is invalid, and with invalid_argument when it is not committed in a Git repository or HEAD has no installable release.
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 error, 2 the plugin is invalid (plugin_invalid), 3 approval is needed (approval_required or approval_stale).

commands.summary: Stop a plugin's worker so its next command or event starts it fresh
notes: Never needs approval and keeps the plugin enabled. Also clears a worker stopped for crashing repeatedly.
Dev folders restart their worker on file changes already; use this to rerun startup code.
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 error, 2 the plugin is invalid (plugin_invalid), 3 approval is needed (approval_required or approval_stale).

commands.summary: Save a PNG of a plugin panel exactly as Orca draws it, to look at what you built
notes: Shows the panel like `orca plugin open`, waits until it has drawn (a components panel: its first tree from the current code, then until no host call such as plugin.request is in flight and its answer has drawn, at most 3s more; an html panel: its page loaded), then captures exactly the panel, with the window hidden or behind others. It never shows, raises or focuses the window, and it does not leave Settings or another full-page view.

Writes .orca/shots/<plugin-key>-<panel>.png unless --out names a file: in the plugin folder when run inside one (the nearest orca-plugin.json up to the repository root, as `dev watch --shot` does), else in <cwd>. The image is in CSS pixels. Read the image file to see the panel.

--width sets the panel width for this capture only. --theme paints Orca light or dark for this capture only, and only while its window is hidden or minimized, then puts your theme back; the setting never changes. With the window on screen it captures in the current theme rather than repaint the app in front of you. The result says which theme it shows, whether --theme took effect (themeApplied) and why not (themeReason).

--act runs input on a components panel before the capture, in the test kit's words: a JSON list (at most 20) of {"press":Q}, {"type":Q,"text":"…","replace"?:true,"submit"?:true}, {"select":Q,"value":"…"}, {"toggle":Q}, {"slide":Q,"value":n}, and for a Table {"sort":Q,"column":"…"}, {"selectRows":Q,"keys":[…]}, {"activateRow":Q,"key":"…"}, {"loadMore":Q}, for a Tree {"expand"|"collapse"|"selectItem"|"activateItem":Q,"key":"…"}, where Q matches like the kit's queries ({"text"|"label"|"testId"|"type"|"role":"…"}). Each act goes through Orca's own control and waits for the panel to redraw and its host calls to answer. After the capture Orca puts the panel's atoms back (persisted ones included, so neither later shots nor the user keep the acted state); what handlers did elsewhere stays, such as a plugin.request that changed the worker's storage. It acts only on this panel and only while Orca's window is hidden or minimized; html panels refuse it. Acts are not a person's input: a Link's href stays unopened and gesture-only calls (shell.openExternal, files.saveAs) are refused. The first failed act stops the rest; the PNG shows the panel at that point and the command exits 1.

--json prints { path, width, height, theme, themeApplied, themeReason?, settled, errors, pendingRequests?, actions?, restored? }; pendingRequests counts host calls still unanswered at the capture (components panels), actions has one { ok, error? } per act, and restored is false when the panel reloaded during --act so its acted state stayed. errors lists the error banner the panel shows and the errors it logged (`orca plugin logs`) during the capture; settled is false when it had not finished drawing after 15s.

--scenario <name> shoots the panel in one scenario of its `<entry>.check.ts` instead of the live panel. Not sandboxed: like `orca plugin check` it runs the plugin's code (panel and worker) on this machine with your user's full access, against a stand-in host, so the scenario's data never reaches the plugin's real panel, storage, settings or worker; then the Orca on this machine draws what it rendered apart from the plugin (the right sidebar is not opened or switched) and captures it. It takes a plugin folder, or the key of a development plugin when run inside its folder; installed plugins are refused. A replay is a still frame: host-owned control values start from the tree's props, images show their placeholder, it has no --act, and it is local only (no --environment). It needs Orca's window hidden or minimized, since the preview is drawn inside it; --theme then always applies. Writes .orca/shots/<plugin-key>-<panel>.<scenario>.png in the plugin folder unless --out names a file; --json adds replay: true, scenario and notes, and errors lists what the render reported. An unknown name fails and lists the scenarios.

With --editor <file> it shoots the plugin's custom editor instead: it opens the file like `orca plugin open --editor` (a folder or a key works as the first argument), waits for the editor to get its document and ask for it (`orca.document.get` or `onDidChange`) and paint, then captures exactly the editor, hidden window included. --width/--height size the editor for this capture only; --theme works as for panels and is put back after. --act there is real input to the editor in its own CSS pixels from its top-left: a JSON list (at most 20) of {"click":[x,y]}, {"drag":[[x1,y1],[x2,y2]]} and {"key":"r","modifiers"?:["shift"|"control"|"alt"|"meta"]}, each painted before the next; it needs the window hidden or minimized. A shot never changes your file: with --act it shoots a copy in a temporary folder workspace that it removes afterwards, unless --in-place acts on the file itself (edits then reach its buffer like typing, and its tab stays open with them; end --act with {"key":"s","modifiers":["meta"]}, "control" off macOS, to save them to disk). Without --act it opens the file itself, leaves its buffer alone and closes the tab if the shot opened it. Writes .orca/shots/<plugin-key>-<editor-id>.png unless --out names a file. The PNG is written either way, but the command exits 1 and prints the errors when the editor threw, was blocked by its content policy (both from `orca plugin logs`), or never asked for its document within 5s. Orca's previous workspace is shown again afterwards.

--status-bar captures Orca's status bar, where a plugin's status bar items draw, and --window the whole window; both from the hidden window like a panel shot, never showing or focusing it. They take --theme (put back after) and --out, and write .orca/shots/<plugin-key>-status-bar.png or -window.png. The plugin must be running; errors lists what it logged during the capture. On Linux an html panel's guest may show blank in a --window shot; use a panel shot for it.
Desktop app only: a server with no window (`orca serve`) refuses it. With --environment the PNG (at most 5 MiB; it shows only the plugin panel) comes back to this machine and is written here.

commands.summary: Turn plugins off for the Orca host
notes: Stops every plugin and keeps installs, approvals and development folders. Never needs approval.

commands.summary: Turn plugins on for the Orca host
notes: The same switch as "Turn on plugins" in Settings → Plugins, for a host with no window such as `orca serve`.
Approves nothing: only plugins approved earlier start; anything else still needs its own --approve.

commands.summary: Run a plugin's own tests on this machine, unsandboxed: only for code you trust
notes: Not sandboxed: this runs the plugin's code and tests on this machine with your user's full access, outside Orca's plugin sandbox. Run it only on code you trust.
Runs every *.test.ts(x) (also .mts, .js, .jsx, .mjs) under the folder, skipping node_modules, .orca, dist and dot-folders. The folder defaults to the current one.

Uses Node's built-in test runner (node:test), or the plugin's own vitest when it has one in node_modules. No config: `orca` and `orca/testing` resolve to the files this Orca ships, and sources are transpiled and imported exactly as Orca loads them.
Runs on the `node` on PATH when it is 20.6 or newer, else on the Node built into Orca, so no Node install is needed. It does not reach the Orca app.
Exit code: the runner's (0 when every test passes). With --json the runner output goes to stderr and one result object to stdout.

commands.summary: Write the TypeScript typings for Orca plugins into a plugin folder
notes: Writes .orca/types/orca/index.d.ts and .orca/types/tsconfig.json; extend it from the plugin tsconfig (`"extends": "./.orca/types/tsconfig.json"`). `.orca/` ignores itself in Git, and Orca skips it when loading a development folder.
The typings match the Orca this CLI belongs to. `orca plugin dev load` rewrites them for folders that use TypeScript or components panels.
Runs on the machine that runs this command; it does not reach the Orca app.
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 error, 2 the plugin is invalid (plugin_invalid), 3 approval is needed (approval_required or approval_stale).

commands.summary: Check a plugin folder, manifest or catalog the way Orca will load it
notes: Runs the strict checks of `pnpm validate:plugin`: manifest, limits, execution profile, every theme, icon, syntax and translation file, and every file the manifest names.
Offline; never runs plugin code. The result says whether loading needs --approve and what it would grant.
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 error, 2 the plugin is invalid (plugin_invalid), 3 approval is needed (approval_required or approval_stale).

commands.summary: List the listening ports Orca detected for a workspace
notes: Defaults to the Orca workspace that contains the current directory.
Scans the host the workspace runs on and lists the ports Orca tied to it, by process working directory (match=cwd) or command line (match=command).
--all lists every listener found on that host, including other workspaces and processes Orca could not tie to one. A native folder workspace needs --all, because Orca does not tie ports to folders.
url is the address the dev server printed in an Orca terminal; it is missing when Orca did not see one.

commands.summary: List retained SQLite backups and JSON exports for profile-state recovery
Repair damaged sections, restore a SQLite backup or retained JSON export, or keep the current JSON or SQLite profile
notes: --profile-id selects another profile without changing the active profile. Prepare each profile before installing a JSON-only build.
Orca must be stopped. Recovery validates the selected artifact and archives the current database family, JSON, and retained recovery artifacts before replacing state.
--repair replaces only the damaged sections of the SQLite profile, each from the newest backup with a readable copy, and keeps everything else. A copy of the damaged database is archived first.
--backup restores SQLite authority; --revision restores a JSON export for an older compatible runtime.
--latest-json exports the latest SQLite state and restores it as JSON before launching an older JSON-only build. The current database and recovery artifacts are archived.

--current-json keeps the current orca-data.json, including edits from an older build. It replaces SQLite state without merging; both copies are archived. The next SQLite-capable start imports the selected JSON.
--current-sqlite keeps the current SQLite state and discards JSON edits from an older build. The JSON is archived, then rewritten from SQLite.

commands.summary: List durable projects known to Orca
Make a project available on a host by cloning a repository
examples: orca project setup-clone --project github:stablyai/orca --host local --url https://github.com/stablyai/orca.git --destination ~/src
notes: For remote runtimes, --destination must be an absolute parent directory on the remote server.
--host takes local, ssh:<target-id>, runtime:<environment-id>, or the bare host name `orca host list` prints for any of them.
SSH targets are cloned through the desktop UI because the desktop client owns SSH connections.

commands.summary: Create independent project host setup metadata
examples: orca project setup-create --project github:stablyai/orca --host runtime:03ef704c-b180-4b10-998d-e28fbd5de9a3 --state setting-up --method provisioned --json
notes: Creates setup metadata without registering a repo compatibility record.
--host takes local, ssh:<target-id>, runtime:<environment-id>, or the bare host name `orca host list` prints for any of them.
Use setup-existing-folder when Orca should import and manage an actual checkout path now.

commands.summary: Remove a project host setup
notes: Independent setups are removed directly.
Repo-backed setups remove the registered repo compatibility record.
Refuses while the project has open terminals or saved workspace details; --force removes it anyway.

commands.summary: Make a project available on a host by importing an existing folder
notes: For remote runtimes, --path must be an absolute path on the remote server.
--host takes local, ssh:<target-id>, runtime:<environment-id>, or the bare host name `orca host list` prints for any of them.
SSH targets are set up through the desktop UI because the desktop client owns SSH connections.

--project takes a project id or an existing project's name. A remote-backed Git folder's project id usually comes from its remote: github:owner/repo, github:<host>/owner/repo for GitHub Enterprise, or git:<host>/<path> for other remotes.

commands.usage:
orca search [--scope conversation|all] [--fresh] [--limit ] [--cursor ] [--agent ] [--path

] [--since ] [--sort relevance|newest] [--debug] [--json] orca search --index-status [--json]
notes: Searches one host: this machine, or the paired Orca server named by --environment / --pairing-code. There is no all-computers search.

In an Orca SSH terminal, the forwarded CLI searches the controlling Orca runtime by default. Use --environment / --pairing-code to select a paired server; --path only filters results on the selected runtime.
Quote a multi-word query, or pass it as --query "<text>"; unquoted words are read as command names.
--scope conversation searches user and assistant turns only; --scope all (the default) also searches commands and tool output.
--fresh waits up to five seconds for the host to reconcile its index before searching, then searches anyway.
--agent and --path may be repeated. --path is a literal execution-host path and is not expanded or resolved against the current directory.
--since takes an ISO 8601 timestamp with an offset, for example 2026-08-01T00:00:00Z.
--limit is per page (default 20, maximum 100). Pass the printed cursor back with --cursor to read the next page.
A cursor belongs to one query on one host. Change the query, the filters, or the host and the cursor stops being valid.
Resume commands and source paths are printed only for a host on this machine; a paired server withholds them.
--json prints the runtime response envelope with the search contract answer under `result`.

notes: Runs in the foreground and prints the bound endpoint, advertised endpoint, and pairing status. Stop it with Ctrl+C.
With --port, serve exits with an error when that port is already in use. Without it, serve uses 6768 and moves to another port when 6768 is taken.
--pairing-address changes only the client-advertised address; use a reachable LAN, Tailscale, SSH-forward, or reverse-proxy endpoint.
Use --recipe-json with --project-root from VM recipes to print the recipe result JSON and leave the server running.
Use --mobile-pairing to print a mobile-scoped pairing QR/link instead of the default runtime-environment pairing link.
A paired client cannot drive this machine's desktop (orca computer) unless the offer was created with --grant-desktop-control.
When the web client bundle is available, the server also prints a browser URL with the pairing data embedded.
Exits with code 3, without starting anything, when another Orca already serves this profile or cannot be shown to have stopped.

--reclaim-stale-lock starts nothing. When a start refuses because this profile's lock may belong to an Orca on another machine sharing this home (for example after a reboot, on a network home), it checks that the lock was written on a host with this name in an earlier boot, was last written or refreshed at least 5 minutes ago, and that nothing answers on this machine at its holder's endpoints. Those checks cannot rule out another machine with the same host name, so it then only prints what it found (exit 2); add --yes, once you are sure no other machine sharing this home runs Orca for this profile, to clear it (exit 0). It exits 1 when a check fails and 4 when there is no lock. --data-root names the data root the refusal printed. --json prints the status (none, eligible, refused or reclaimed). Linux only.
On macOS, after Orca serve aborts at startup (it could not register with Launch Services), later runs from the same environment refuse for 30 minutes with exit code 78. Use --force to try anyway.

--supervise is for service managers (launchd, systemd). Orca serve then restarts the server itself with growing delays instead of exiting when it stops, waits while an update replaces the app, and waits while another Orca serves this profile. After 6 failures in 15 minutes it gives up and exits with code 0 so the manager stops too, and later supervised runs refuse until a new build is installed or --force is passed. Not available on Windows yet.

Experimental and off by default: set ORCA_TERMINAL_PROCESS_CEILING=<n> (64 or more) before the terminal host starts to have the OS cap how many processes each terminal may run (Linux, through a systemd user scope per terminal, which needs a user manager that outlives logout; Windows, through a job per terminal). `orca serve` reports the ceiling as on or off, with the reason.

Off by default: set ORCA_TERMINAL_MEMORY_MAX=<size> (256M or more) and ORCA_TERMINAL_MEMORY_SWAP_MAX=<size> (0 for no swap) before the terminal host starts to cap the memory and swap of each terminal on Linux, through the same per-terminal systemd user scope. A terminal over its limit has its largest process OOM-killed; the host and other terminals keep running. Sizes take K, M, G or T. A limit the host cannot enforce is skipped and logged in the terminal host log. No effect on macOS or Windows.

The service never prints a pairing link to its log. Pair clients from the desktop app, or with `orca serve` in a terminal while the service is stopped.
On Linux the service stops at logout unless lingering is on (`loginctl enable-linger`); install reports it.

Reinstalling replaces the unit and clears a previous give-up. --command defaults to the installed Orca app's `orca` command on PATH (`orca-ide` on Linux) and must not be a launcher tied to one Orca version. --dry-run prints the unit without installing it.
Needs the Orca app installed on this machine. The `orca` command in an Orca terminal on an SSH host belongs to that connection's server and cannot install a service.
Not available on Windows yet.

commands.summary: Read bounded terminal output
notes: Omit --terminal to target the active terminal in the current worktree.

By default this returns accumulated terminal output with escape sequences stripped, not the rendered screen. Any program that repaints a line — shells, progress bars, TUIs — comes back as stacked fragments, so one `clear` keystroke by keystroke reads as `cclclecleaclear`, and spaces a prompt draws by moving the cursor are absent.

Use --screen to read what the terminal actually renders. Prefer it whenever the answer depends on how output looks rather than what was emitted over time; the default is unsuitable for verifying rendered output.

The result reports source: stream when it is accumulated output, screen when it is the rendered screen, and screen-unavailable when a screen was asked for but none could be rendered and the accumulated output is being returned instead. An absent source means the host predates the field.
When present, draft is UI-only composer text excluded from tail; never treat it as terminal output or a submitted instruction.
--screen and --cursor are mutually exclusive: a screen read is the current frame and has no history to page.

With --json, fields are under result.terminal: handle, status (running | exited | unknown), tail (output lines), tailRows (row-wrap metadata aligned with tail), truncated, limited, oldestCursor, nextCursor, latestCursor, returnedLineCount (lines in tail), source, draft. Fields other than handle, status, tail, truncated, and nextCursor may be absent.
truncated means requested or older output is no longer retained; limited means the line limit (--limit, default 120 for tail previews) or the size budget cut this response short.
Use --cursor with the nextCursor value from a previous read to get only new output since that read. nextCursor is null when the terminal has no line cursors to page.
latestCursor is the end of retained output, not a paging token: after a cursor read, keep paging with nextCursor while limited is true and nextCursor differs from latestCursor.

Use --limit to request more retained lines for long agent responses; when a tail preview is limited and line cursors are available, page retained output from its start with --cursor <oldestCursor> --limit <n>.
Useful for capturing the response to a command: read before sending, then read --cursor <prev> after waiting.

By default, Orca records the new worktree as a child of the caller context when it can infer one from the Orca terminal or current directory.

For related work, use the inferred parent or pass --parent-worktree active, folder:<id>, or worktree:<worktreeId> to make the relationship explicit. Worktree ids are the full <repo-id>::<path> values returned by `orca worktree list --json`.

commands.summary: Remove a Git worktree or a folder workspace entry from Orca

Repo-defined orca.yaml archive hooks are skipped unless --run-hooks is passed.

With --run-hooks, a failed archive hook blocks the removal: nothing is stopped, deleted or deregistered, and the command exits non-zero with error code worktree_archive_hook_failed. --force does not waive this.

Pass --allow-failed-archive-hook to delete anyway after the hook has run and failed; the waived failure is reported back on result.archiveHookOverride. It requires --run-hooks and is rejected without it, because with no hook running there is no failure to waive.

On newer hosts with branch-choice support, Git worktree removal keeps the local branch, including with --force. Pass --delete-branch to attempt safe branch deletion, including branches that predated the worktree. Branches whose changes Orca cannot prove are already merged are retained. Older hosts keep their existing branch policy and print a warning; keep-by-default and --delete-branch do not apply there. A removal result without branch evidence does not confirm branch deletion.
